entries.title: One hand holds, the other turns
entries.summary: Davies describes a basic nuts-and-bolts activity with one or two shaped pairs, starting with the nuts already attached. Small parts need adult supervision.
entries.cue: Your child may be interested in holding something steady while turning another part.
detail: In this early example, each nut corresponds to the shape of its bolt. The child can explore the turning movement without first finding the right place to start the nut.
Her activity chapter describes one hand holding a bolt while the other turns its nut. Show a small movement slowly when help is welcome, and leave time to repeat it.
The photographed board for grading different sizes is a separate, later example from around 2 years. The basic pair does not call for that whole set.

entries.title: Two hands working on a bead
entries.summary: Davies describes threading as a way to explore what two hands can do together. Bead size and thread thickness follow the child’s ability, with an adult supervising small parts.
entries.cue: Your child may be interested in guiding a thread through a bead and finding it on the other side.
detail: Her illustrated threading example is from 16 months. In the appendix, the 16–18+ month row begins with five or six wooden beads and plastic tubing that can be pushed a little way through a bead.

Her chapter also describes a lace with a firm wooden end before an ordinary shoelace. These are different material examples; choose a manageable challenge rather than trying to follow every variation.
A child can repeat one small part, accept a slow demonstration, or leave it for another time. The later examples with small beads and thin thread are not a requirement to make this activity harder.

entries.title: Explore a fastening before getting dressed
entries.summary: Davies’s dressing frames let a child repeat one fastening movement separately from putting on clothes. Help stays available, and the frames are examples rather than a required collection.
entries.cue: Your child may return to pulling apart Velcro or moving a zipper.
detail: The early appendix examples use two pieces of fabric on a wooden frame: Velcro from 14+ months, and a zipper from 16–18+ months. In the zipper example, the fabric stays joined at the bottom.
Her later frames use large buttons or snap fasteners from 18–22+ months and buckles from 2½ years. Those labels describe different possibilities, not a sequence every child must complete.

Show slowly if the child wants help and let them repeat the part that interests them. Small parts require supervision. Managing a fastening during play does not remove the help a child may want while dressing.

entries.title: A turn to add and stir
entries.summary: When you have time to bake together, Davies includes a young toddler in adding ingredients the adult has measured and stirring with a wooden spoon. The shared process can be one small part.
entries.cue: Your child may watch you mix or reach to join the movement.
detail: Her baking caption gives these forms of help from 12 months. The adult has already measured the ingredients; the child can help add them or take a turn mixing.

For children under 2, she suggests keeping practical tasks to one or two steps and adding more only as they become manageable. The work will take longer, and you can stop before either of you feels overwhelmed.
The appendix’s later baking row, from 2½ years, includes helping measure ingredients. That is a different part of baking. This early invitation stays with adding and stirring alongside an adult.

entries.title: Talk about a recurring night need during the day
entries.summary: Davies suggests returning to repeated nighttime requests at a calm daytime moment. The adult and child can think together about what might help, while keeping the child’s need for support in view.
entries.cue: The same request for a cuddle, drink, cover adjustment or familiar toy keeps coming up at night.
detail: The conversation happens at a neutral time, when the family can notice what was difficult and consider an idea together. In her wider problem-solving approach, even a preverbal toddler can contribute through an action or gesture; the adult may supply most possibilities.

This does not mean the child must manage the night alone. Davies’s sleep chapter keeps the help the child needs, rejects leaving a child to cry alone, and makes room for extra support during illness or teething.
If continuing sleep difficulties affect the well-being of the child or family, Davies advises seeing a sleep specialist.
